title: Ukraine Combats AI Cyberattacks
content:
Hackers associated with the FSB secret service or the Russian General Staff are unleashing AI tools to break into Ukrainian IT networks. Once inside, Russian AI agents move on their own from machine to machine and report back to human operators, who then decide whether to steal data, plant malware, or shut down the service.  

AI allows for cheap, fast cyber-attacks. While hackers previously used the technology for isolated tasks like writing phishing emails, AI is behind a 2500% increase in low-severity attacks for the first half of 2026, compared to the previous year.

Targets range from law enforcement agencies to private notaries and medical institutions. Some attacks jam military mobile devices. Others generate fake air raid alerts. And still others steal geolocation, photos, contacts, and call logs.

title: Solar Surprise: Dealing with a Surplus
content:
Spain and China share a common problem: they produce too much solar power. 

The two countries are committed to a green future and have made dizzying progress. Over the past two years, Chinese renewables exceeded ten trillion kWh of electricity for the first time and are expected to account for a third of growth in global demand by 2040, driven by its ever-expanding electric car fleet, industrial transformation, and artificial intelligence data centers.

Although my home country of Spain is much smaller than China, it too is experiencing a renewable boom. More than $80 billion in capital has been invested over the last 15 years in renewables, with solar costs dropping from $0.36/kWh in 2010 to just $0.04/kWh. Green energy accounts for two-thirds of the total national power grid. 

The price of solar panels has fallen by roughly 90% over the last decade. Solar is not dependent on moving parts that wear out, and production can be managed with software, without the need to maintain turbines or furnaces.
snippet: Spain and China share a common problem: they produce too much solar power.
creator: Jack Galloway

title: Russia’s Ominous Migrant Weaponization
content:
Russia’s shadow war against Europe is a multiple pronged attack on NATO and other countries. In the northeastern sector of this front line, shoving developing world migrants through border fences has long played a role. In October, this campaign took a new and ominous turn.

On October 6, masked and armed individuals tried to drive at least 20 migrants from Belarus into Latvia, threatening the Latvian soldiers confronting them, according to the public media account. Hours later, masked people again crossed into Latvia, damaged an electricity distribution box, stole surveillance cameras and returned to Belarus before border guards arrived.

Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava warned that Belarus should expect serious consequences. This was not another episode of migration pressure but an armed intimidation and sabotage to a route already being used to pressure Latvia’s border. About 1,000 migrants monthly attempt to cross the frontier with Belarusian assistance.

title: Spheres of Influence Won’t Help the US
content:
In February 1991, officials of the Warsaw Pact gathered for a final meeting in Budapest.

When the doors opened and Soviet officials and officers emerged with delegates from the five other member states, there was an expression of barely suppressed hilarity on the faces of many. A journalist approached one Central European delegation to ask why.

The officials could barely contain themselves. “As the meeting was ending,” one said, “the Russians said there was one final thing – no one had said thank you.”

“Thank you? Asked one delegate. “What for”

“A thank you for keeping the peace all these years.”

Czechs, Slovaks and Hungarians, whose countries had been invaded by Russian tanks, were said to have led the snorts of derision and suppressed laughter. This was too much for the Russians, who packed up their papers and left.

title: Western Embassies Must Stay in Bomb-Blasted Kyiv
content:
Some Western diplomats in Kyiv have reportedly begun contingency planning to relocate to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russian attacks on the capital intensify further. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry later said that no diplomatic mission had formally notified it of plans to leave Kyiv.

The reports may never translate into actual relocation, but they highlight a potentially much bigger problem: what happens if Russia’s growing pressure on the capital succeeds in persuading Ukraine’s international partners to abandon Kyiv, as many did in 2022?

That question has become more urgent as Moscow’s campaign against Kyiv grows increasingly disruptive. Recent strikes have hit energy infrastructure and the bridges connecting the two banks of the Dnipro. More than a third of Kyiv’s residents live on the left bank while many work on the right, making these crossings central to the city’s daily functioning.

title: Turkey and Azerbaijan: Old Allies Fall Out
content:
The close relationship between Turkey and Azerbaijan has been a reliable and longstanding feature of geopolitics at the often-disputatious junction of Europe and Asia.

The 2021 Shusha Declaration formalized a relationship that had provided Azerbaijan with the drones and other equipment to defeat Armenian forces in Nagorno-Karabakh the previous year. It extended Turkish influence into the South Caucasus and crowned Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan as a powerful figure in the region.

Is that really now at risk from a dispute over girls’ schoolwear?

On 12 October, the Azerbaijani government introduced new school uniform regulations that effectively barred hijab-wearing female students from attending classes, triggering public criticism and protests in several schools. While authorities cited Azerbaijan’s constitutional commitment to secularism and its long-standing secular traditions, the decision has exposed deep societal divisions, with some segments of the public supporting the policy and others viewing it as a restriction on religious freedom.

title: Ukraine’s Medical Evacuations Go Airborne
content:
A recent video released by Ukraine’s 92nd Assault Brigade reportedly showed a heavy bomber drone helping to evacuate a soldier, in what was the world’s first attempt to use a drone for the mission. “Due to high enemy drone activity and mined terrain, evacuating him using traditional unmanned ground systems was impossible,” said the brigade.

The soldier, Kostiantyn Vlasenko, had been cut off for months and had lost a leg. In the end, alone and fearing gangrene, he decided to amputate the other. Earlier attempts to reach him had failed.

Ukraine has been testing medical evacuations with aerial drones throughout this year and had previously used ground robots.

“This is the first time in human history that such an operation has been carried out,” says Anatolii, a commander of a mortar battery unit from the unit. “I think we’ll see it happen more often, but everything will depend on the conditions . . . [it works best] in rain or fog.”

The widespread use of drones across the front, and the expansion of the kill zone, moving in and out and getting the wounded evacuated from the front has become a very dangerous job.
snippet: A recent video released by Ukraine’s 92nd Assault Brigade reportedly showed a heavy bomber drone helping to evacuate a soldier, in what was the world’s first attempt to use a drone for the mission.
creator: David Kirichenko

title: A Silicon Curtain Is Descending Across the Semiconductor World
content:
The annual ISSCC Forum is dubbed the “Olympics of Chips.”  As a young engineer, I attended. Despite intense commercial competition, the global forum wowed me. The brightest minds from MIT, Stanford, Cambridge, and elsewhere competed with engineers from major chip firms for attention to their breakthroughs in solid-state circuits and systems-on-a-chip. 

This year’s forum in San Francisco featured MediaTek’s Rick Tsai from Taiwan, IBM’s Heike Riel, Cadence’s Anirudh Devgan, and Apple’s Hope Giles. But the public program listed no plenary speaker from a major Chinese chip or AI company.

Global technical exchange and commercial networking built the chip industry. Engineers, chipmakers, equipment suppliers, customers, and investors met at the same conferences and trade shows. That cooperative international circuit is now broken into a world of rival technology industries, with democratic semiconductor powers pitted against authoritarian China.

title: Pen Pushers Help Engineers Keep Ukraine’s Lights On
content:
Russia’s campaign against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure is forcing the country to rethink a system built around large power plants and long transmission lines. The answer is increasingly decentralized generation: smaller gas-fired units, cogeneration, batteries, modular boiler houses, renewables, and backup systems closer to consumers.

Kyiv has been expanding smaller, distributed sources of electricity and heat, alongside storage and backup generation, to make energy supply less vulnerable to Russian strikes. But it still depends on local implementation.

The decisive question will be if Ukraine’s municipalities have the institutional capacity to turn money, equipment, and plans into functioning systems.

In March, comprehensive resilience plans for regions and regional centers were approved. They focused on protection of critical infrastructure, development of distributed generation, backup and alternative power, and decentralization of heat generation. Kyiv said these were long-term measures to strengthen communities beyond a single winter.

title: Could China and Russia Rescue Cuba’s Regime?
content:
The energy blockade has become the principal instrument of pressure employed by Washington against the Cuban regime. Unlike other coercive measures, restrictions on hydrocarbons directly affect the country’s ability to function and have resulted in repeated and lengthy nationwide power cuts.

The strategy became particularly significant after the overthrow and capture of Nicolás Maduro in January, which enabled the US to disrupt oil shipments from Venezuela, one of the principal sources of support for Cuba’s economy. Washington also put pressure on Mexico, which had become an increasingly important energy supplier to the island.

President Donald Trump’s January 29 executive order, which established a mechanism for imposing additional tariffs on countries supplying oil to Cuba, joined together sanctions on key sectors of the Cuban economy in a strategy intended to increase the costs of sustaining the communist regime from abroad.

But the effectiveness of the blockade depends on Washington’s ability to deter other states from providing Havana with the resources it needs.
